title: Acts 25:1–27
context: The new governor Festus visits Jerusalem, where the chief priests ask him to bring Paul there, planning to ambush him. Festus hears the case in Caesarea, where the accusers bring serious but unproven charges. When Festus, wanting to please the Jews, asks whether Paul will stand trial in Jerusalem, Paul appeals to Caesar, and Festus grants the appeal. King Agrippa and Bernice arrive, and Festus explains that the dispute concerns their religion and a dead man named Jesus whom Paul claims is alive. Agrippa asks to hear Paul, and the next day Festus presents him to the assembled dignitaries, admitting he has nothing definite to write to the emperor.

verses.text: Festus therefore, having come into the province, after three days went up to Jerusalem from Caesarea.
verses.arminianNotes: Three days after arriving in his province, Festus goes up from Caesarea to Jerusalem. A new governor would want to meet the Jewish leadership quickly.
verses.reformedNotes: Festus governed briefly, from about AD 59 to 62, and Josephus remembers him as more just than Felix or his successors.

verses.text: Then the high priest and the principal men of the Jews informed him against Paul, and they begged him,
verses.arminianNotes: The high priest and leading men immediately bring their case against Paul. Two years have not cooled their determination.
verses.reformedNotes: The persistence of the accusers shows that the case has always been about Paul’s message rather than any civil offense.

verses.text: asking a favor against him, that he would summon him to Jerusalem, plotting to kill him on the way.
verses.arminianNotes: They ask as a favor that Paul be transferred to Jerusalem, planning to ambush him on the way. The plot of 23:12–15 is revived.
verses.reformedNotes: They try to use a new governor’s desire for goodwill to accomplish what the earlier conspiracy could not.

verses.text: However Festus answered that Paul should be kept in custody at Caesarea, and that he himself was about to depart shortly.
verses.arminianNotes: Festus answers that Paul is being kept at Caesarea and that he himself will return there soon.
verses.reformedNotes: A simple administrative decision closes the door on the ambush. Luke shows the promise of 23:11 protected again.

verses.text: “Let them therefore”, he said, “that are in power among you go down with me, and if there is anything wrong in the man, let them accuse him.”
verses.arminianNotes: “Let your leading men come down with me, and if there is anything wrong in the man, let them accuse him.” Festus insists on a proper hearing.
verses.reformedNotes: Roman procedure, with its requirement that accusers face the accused, keeps working in Paul’s favor.

verses.text: When he had stayed among them more than ten days, he went down to Caesarea, and on the next day he sat on the judgment seat, and commanded Paul to be brought.
verses.arminianNotes: After eight or ten days Festus returns to Caesarea and, the next day, takes his seat on the tribunal and orders Paul brought.
verses.reformedNotes: The bema, the judge’s seat, signals a formal Roman trial.

verses.text: When he had come, the Jews who had come down from Jerusalem stood around him, bringing against him many and grievous charges which they could not prove,
verses.arminianNotes: The Jews from Jerusalem surround Paul and bring many serious charges they cannot prove.
verses.reformedNotes: Luke does not list the charges; the repeated failure of proof is the point.

verses.text: while he said in his defense, “Neither against the law of the Jews, nor against the temple, nor against Caesar, have I sinned at all.”
verses.arminianNotes: Paul answers in one sentence: he has committed no offense against the Jewish law, the temple, or Caesar. The three charges are religious, cultic, and political.
verses.reformedNotes: Paul’s summary denial covers each realm of authority. Luke presents him as a loyal Jew and a law-abiding subject.

verses.text: But Festus, desiring to gain favor with the Jews, answered Paul and said, “Are you willing to go up to Jerusalem and be judged by me there concerning these things?”
verses.arminianNotes: Festus, wanting to do the Jews a favor, asks whether Paul is willing to go to Jerusalem to be tried there before him.
verses.reformedNotes: The question puts Paul’s life at risk to buy political goodwill, and Paul recognizes the danger at once.

verses.text: But Paul said, “I am standing before Caesar’s judgment seat, where I ought to be tried. I have done no wrong to the Jews, as you also know very well.
verses.arminianNotes: Paul replies that he is standing before Caesar’s tribunal, where he ought to be tried, and that he has done no wrong to the Jews, as Festus knows very well.
verses.reformedNotes: Paul insists on the court with lawful jurisdiction. Reformed writers have long drawn from this the legitimacy of appealing to civil authority for justice.

verses.text: For if I have done wrong and have committed anything worthy of death, I don’t refuse to die; but if none of those things is true that they accuse me of, no one can give me up to them. I appeal to Caesar!”
verses.arminianNotes: If he has done something deserving death, he does not refuse to die; but if the charges are empty, no one can hand him over. “I appeal to Caesar.” A citizen’s right of provocatio moved the case to the emperor, then Nero.
verses.reformedNotes: The appeal becomes the means by which God brings Paul to Rome. Paul acts on his legal rights, and through that act the promise of 23:11 moves forward.

verses.text: Then Festus, when he had conferred with the council, answered, “You have appealed to Caesar. To Caesar you shall go.”
verses.arminianNotes: After consulting his council, Festus answers: “You have appealed to Caesar. To Caesar you shall go.”
verses.reformedNotes: A Roman governor’s formal ruling now carries the apostle toward the capital. Luke lets the official words echo God’s earlier “must.”

verses.text: Now when some days had passed, King Agrippa and Bernice arrived at Caesarea and greeted Festus.
verses.arminianNotes: Some days later King Agrippa II and his sister Bernice arrive in Caesarea to welcome Festus. Agrippa ruled territories north and east of Galilee and oversaw the temple and high priestly appointments.
verses.reformedNotes: Jesus had said his witnesses would stand before kings (Luke 21:12), and the Lord told Ananias that Paul would bear his name before kings (9:15).

verses.text: As he stayed there many days, Festus laid Paul’s case before the king, saying, “There is a certain man left a prisoner by Felix;
verses.arminianNotes: Because they stay many days, Festus lays Paul’s case before the king. He wants an expert’s help with a puzzling prisoner.
verses.reformedNotes: Agrippa, raised in Rome and familiar with Jewish affairs, was an obvious adviser.

verses.text: about whom, when I was at Jerusalem, the chief priests and the elders of the Jews informed me, asking for a sentence against him.
verses.arminianNotes: Festus recounts how the chief priests and elders asked for a sentence against Paul when he was in Jerusalem.
verses.reformedNotes: His retelling shows how the case looks from a Roman administrator’s point of view.

verses.text: I answered them that it is not the custom of the Romans to give up any man to destruction before the accused has met the accusers face to face and has had opportunity to make his defense concerning the matter laid against him.
verses.arminianNotes: He told them that Romans do not hand anyone over before he has met his accusers face to face and had a chance to defend himself.
verses.reformedNotes: Festus presents himself as a defender of due process. The principle is good even if his own motives were mixed.

verses.text: When therefore they had come together here, I didn’t delay, but on the next day sat on the judgment seat and commanded the man to be brought.
verses.arminianNotes: He convened the court without delay the next day and ordered Paul brought.
verses.reformedNotes: Festus emphasizes his own promptness to Agrippa.

verses.text: When the accusers stood up, they brought no charges against him of such things as I supposed;
verses.arminianNotes: When the accusers stood up, they brought no charge of the evil he had expected.
verses.reformedNotes: Festus assumed a serious crime and found none. The case has never matched its intensity.

verses.text: but had certain questions against him about their own religion and about one Jesus, who was dead, whom Paul affirmed to be alive.
verses.arminianNotes: Instead they had points of dispute about their own religion and about a certain Jesus, who was dead, whom Paul asserted to be alive.
verses.reformedNotes: A pagan governor sums up the gospel’s core claim with casual precision: the dispute is whether Jesus, who died, is alive.

verses.text: Being perplexed how to inquire concerning these things, I asked whether he was willing to go to Jerusalem and there be judged concerning these matters.
verses.arminianNotes: Unsure how to investigate such questions, he asked if Paul would go to Jerusalem.
verses.reformedNotes: Festus admits his confusion, though he leaves out his wish to please the Jews (25:9).

verses.text: But when Paul had appealed to be kept for the decision of the emperor, I commanded him to be kept until I could send him to Caesar.”
verses.arminianNotes: When Paul appealed to be held for the emperor’s decision, Festus ordered him kept until he could send him to Caesar.
verses.reformedNotes: The appeal is irreversible. The path to Rome is now fixed in law.

verses.text: Agrippa said to Festus, “I also would like to hear the man myself.” “Tomorrow,” he said, “you shall hear him.”
verses.arminianNotes: Agrippa says he would like to hear the man himself. Festus answers, “Tomorrow you shall hear him.”
verses.reformedNotes: The request recalls Herod Antipas’s wish to see Jesus (Luke 23:8). Luke draws the parallel between the two trials.

verses.text: So on the next day, when Agrippa and Bernice had come with great pomp, and they had entered into the place of hearing with the commanding officers and the principal men of the city, at the command of Festus, Paul was brought in.
verses.arminianNotes: The next day Agrippa and Bernice enter the audience hall with great pomp, accompanied by tribunes and leading men of the city.
verses.reformedNotes: Luke contrasts royal display with the chained prisoner whose message outlasts them all.

verses.text: Festus said, “King Agrippa, and all men who are here present with us, you see this man about whom all the multitude of the Jews petitioned me, both at Jerusalem and here, crying that he ought not to live any longer.
verses.arminianNotes: Festus presents Paul as the man about whom the whole Jewish people petitioned, shouting that he ought not to live any longer.
verses.reformedNotes: Festus exaggerates the unanimity, but the description shows how much was at stake for Paul.

verses.text: But when I found that he had committed nothing worthy of death, and as he himself appealed to the emperor, I determined to send him,
verses.arminianNotes: He found that Paul had done nothing worthy of death, and since Paul appealed to the emperor, he decided to send him.
verses.reformedNotes: Another Roman official declares Paul innocent. Like Pilate with Jesus, Festus finds no fault yet does not release him.

verses.text: of whom I have no certain thing to write to my lord. Therefore I have brought him out before you, and especially before you, King Agrippa, that, after examination I may have something to write.
verses.arminianNotes: He has nothing definite to write to “my lord,” the emperor, so he brings Paul before them all, especially Agrippa, to have something to write after the examination.
verses.reformedNotes: Sending a prisoner to Caesar without a clear charge was an embarrassment. The hearing is partly to save Festus’s face.

verses.text: For it seems to me unreasonable, in sending a prisoner, not to also specify the charges against him.”
verses.arminianNotes: It seems unreasonable to send a prisoner without stating the charges against him.
verses.reformedNotes: Festus’s dilemma highlights the emptiness of the case: an appeal to the emperor with nothing to report.
